Marcus —

Thanks for taking this forward. As part of Sigma Health's vendor evaluation we need a concise but technical response to a few performance-related items before we finalize the lab phase. We're particularly focused on real-world stability under mixed workloads and predictable tail behavior. Can you confirm the following and include any evidence you can share: 

1) Recommended test harness and synthesis method for mixed chat (small messages) + long generation (200–1,000 token) traffic so we can reproduce.
2) Typical P50/P95/P99 generation latencies for a standard 2‑B and 13‑B open weights family model at 256 and 512 token outputs on a single dedicated GPU instance. Please state warm vs cold start.
3) Guidance on batch sizing and when batching will increase tail latency vs throughput (we want a safe default config).
4) Failure and graceful degradation behavior: what fallback chains do you recommend when replicas saturate? How does prefix/KV cache affect cold-start recovery?
5) Any lab artifacts you can share: harness scripts, synthetic traffic profiles, sample logs (no customer data).

Procurement also asked for timeline constraints: our security & procurement gates require perf evidence within 7 business days after initial harness handoff. Is that feasible?

Appreciate the granularity — our technical committee will review line-by-line.

—Natalie

Natalie —

Attaching the harness spec (redwood-bakeoff-harness-spec-v1.xlsx) and a simple prime-and-burst script (prime-and-burst-script.sh). High level notes below — Rafael will attach sample logs and a short explanation for the latency numbers.

Recommended harness (summary):
- Two traffic streams: chat (0–64 token prompts, 1–3 response tokens typical) at 65% of QPS; long-gen (200–1,000 token outputs) at 35% of QPS. Use a Poisson arrival process with overlaid periodic bursts to mimic batch-cold spikes.
- Sequence length distributions: include a 1.5x tail multiplier (i.e., 5% of requests >= 800 tokens) to reveal tail sensitivity.
- Warm start conditioning: run a 10-minute steady-state run at 10% of target concurrency with cache priming sequences from a provided seed set; then run 20-minute ramp to target QPS.
- Measurement windows: capture per-request timing (scheduling, queue, kernel, total) and host/GPU metrics at 1s granularity. Export logs in JSONL.

Safe default batching: for mixed workloads we recommend dynamic batching with an upper bound of 32 tokens-per-batch and a max latency budget of 120ms per batch. Practically:
- Low concurrency (<50 concurrent requests): disable cross-request batching for short chat to avoid head-of-line blocking; enable intra-request operator fusion.
- Medium/high concurrency: enable adaptive batching with per-route latency SLOs; set batch max tokens=32, batch timeout=20ms.

Graceful degradation/fallbacks:
- Primary: scale replicas (autoscale threshold at 70% sustained GPU util over 30s).
- Secondary: fall back to a lower-cost quantized model variant pinned to same API route (lossy but preserves shape).
- Tertiary: region fallback to a compatible endpoint (if enabled) and return a 503 with Retry-After header while streaming partial tokens when applicable.

Prefix/KV cache note: the KV cache dramatically reduces work for long-context repeated sessions; however, cache population increases cold-start variance. Our lab will measure cold-start by explicitly clearing KV and measuring time to reach steady-state for representative sessions. Expect ~1.8–2.5x higher P99 on first session for long-context models before cache warms.

I've attached the harness and simple scripts. Rafael, over to you for the measured baselines and example logs.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference

Natalie —

Attaching a small sample of anonymized logs (latency-sample-logs.tar.gz) and summarizing the baseline numbers from our internal runs on A100-class hardware with two model families (2B and 13B open-family). These are baseline lab runs (single replica) with cache primed unless called out as cold-start.

Baseline (single replica, warm):
- 2B model, 256-token generation: P50=18ms, P95=62ms, P99=110ms (throughput ~220 tokens/s sustained)
- 2B model, 512-token generation: P50=33ms, P95=120ms, P99=210ms (throughput ~180 tokens/s)
- 13B model, 256-token generation: P50=45ms, P95=160ms, P99=320ms (throughput ~90 tokens/s)
- 13B model, 512-token generation: P50=82ms, P95=300ms, P99=580ms (throughput ~55 tokens/s)

Cold-start delta (single cold request after cache clear):
- Measured P99 increases: 2B ~+1.6x, 13B ~+2.1x for long-gen (>=256 tokens). Short chat requests show smaller deltas (~+1.2x).

Batching guidance detail:
- We observed that cross-request batching improves average throughput up to 1.8x at high QPS but can widen P99 by up to 1.7x if batch timeout is aggressive (>=50ms).
- For mixed chat+long, adaptive batching with conservative timeout (<=20ms) retained most throughput benefits while limiting tail blow-up.

Failure scenarios and recommended mitigations tested in lab:
- Replica saturation: prioritized shedding to quantized variant (degradation mode) with circuit-breaker that preserves request routing and emits a diagnostics header X-Redwood-Degraded=true.
- Rapid spike beyond autoscale window: if scale cannot catch up within 60s, stream partial tokens and return a short notice banner in response explaining degraded quality.
- Hardware preemption: in multi-tenant Dedicated pools we hot-restart VM-level tasks and reattach caches where possible; this introduces a transient 5–15s window of increased latency which we measure and tag.

Artifacts included: short-run JSONL logs, per-request timing histograms (CSV), and the small shell script to reproduce the prime-and-burst pattern. We redact party-identifying content; logs focus on timing and GPU metrics.

If you'd like, we can provide a quick 60‑minute remote lab session where we run your provided seed prompts against our harness and walk through the results in real time.

-Rafael
